# Write your first GitHub README in 15 minutes

**Hook:**
You’ve just started a new coding project and want to share it with others. A README file is the friendly front door to your project, but writing one from scratch feels overwhelming. With GitHub Copilot’s help, you can build a clear, professional README in about 15 minutes—no prior experience needed.

## Before you start
- A **GitHub account** (free at [github.com](https://github.com))
- A **new or existing repository** on GitHub (you can create one in under 2 minutes)
- A **web browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, or Safari)
- **GitHub Copilot** enabled on your account (free for individuals; check your plan at [github.com/features/copilot](https://github.com/features/copilot))
- **Total time**: ~15 minutes

> ⚠️ GitHub Copilot is a paid feature on most plans. The free trial may offer limited suggestions. If you see a “Try Copilot for free” prompt, follow it.

---

## Step 1 — Open your repository and start the README file
Open your repository on GitHub in your browser. You’ll land on the main page showing your project files. Look for a list of files; if you just created the repo, you may see only a `.gitignore` file or nothing yet. At the top-right of the file list, click **Add file** and choose **Create new file**. Name the file `README.md`. The `.md` stands for “Markdown,” a simple way to format text with symbols like `#` for headings.

You’ll see a blank editor with a placeholder: “Write a new file in …”. The file name `README.md` tells GitHub this is the project’s welcome page.

💬 Example:
`README.md`

You'll know it worked when you see the filename `README.md` at the top of the editor and the page title says “Create new file”.

---

## Step 2 — Ask Copilot to generate the README structure
With the file open, press the **Ask Copilot** button (usually a chat icon or a sparkle) in the top-right corner of the editor. If you don’t see it, look for a **Copilot** icon in the toolbar or a **Ctrl+I** (Windows/Linux) or **Cmd+I** (Mac) shortcut. A chat panel opens on the right.

In the chat box, type:
💬 Example:
Create a README.md structure for a beginner-friendly Python project that counts words in a text file. Include sections for Description, Features, Installation, Usage, License, and Contributing.

Press Enter. Copilot will respond with a suggested structure using Markdown headings like `# Description`, `## Features`, etc. It may also add a short placeholder paragraph under each heading.

You'll know it worked when you see a list of headings and brief descriptions appear in the editor, replacing the blank page.

---

## Step 3 — Fill in the project description
Scroll to the `# Description` section Copilot created. Replace the placeholder text with a clear, one-sentence explanation of your project. For example, if your project is a Python script that counts words, write:

💬 Example:
This simple Python script reads a text file and counts the number of words, lines, and characters. It’s designed for beginners learning file handling and basic data analysis.

You'll know it worked when the description reads like a friendly introduction and fits naturally under the heading.

---

## Step 4 — List the project’s features
Under the `## Features` heading, Copilot likely added a bullet list. Replace each bullet with a short, active phrase describing what your project does. For a word counter, it might look like:

💬 Example:
- Counts words, lines, and characters in any text file
- Works with `.txt` files on Windows, macOS, and Linux
- Lightweight and runs in seconds
- No external libraries required

You'll know it worked when the list clearly shows what the project can do, using simple language.

---

## Step 5 — Add installation instructions
Scroll to the `## Installation` section. Copilot usually suggests commands like `pip install` or `git clone`. Replace the placeholder with step-by-step instructions for your operating system. For a beginner-friendly Python project, write:

💬 Example:
1. Make sure you have Python 3.8 or newer installed. Open your terminal or command prompt and run:
   python --version
   If you see Python 3.x, you’re good to go.
2. Download or clone this project:
   git clone https://github.com/your-username/your-repo.git
3. Move into the project folder:
   cd your-repo
4. Install the required package (if any):
   pip install -r requirements.txt
   (If there’s no `requirements.txt`, skip this step.)

You'll know it worked when the instructions are clear enough for someone with basic computer skills to follow without confusion.

---

## Step 6 — Write a usage example
Under the `## Usage` heading, Copilot often adds a code block with a command like `python wordcounter.py`. Replace it with a simple, copy-paste-ready example. For a word counter, write:

💬 Example:
To count words in a file named `sample.txt`, run:
python wordcounter.py sample.txt

You'll know it worked when the example is short, uses real file names, and shows exactly what to type.

---

## Step 7 — Choose a license and add it
Scroll to the `## License` section. Copilot may suggest a placeholder like “MIT License” or “Apache 2.0”. Replace it with a short explanation and a link to the license file. For beginners, the MIT License is simple and widely used. Write:

💬 Example:
This project is licensed under the MIT License — see the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file for details.

You'll know it worked when the license section clearly states the license type and links to a file named `LICENSE` in your repo.

---

## Step 8 — Add a contribution guide
Under the `## Contributing` heading, Copilot usually adds a short paragraph. Replace it with a beginner-friendly invitation. For example:

💬 Example:
Contributions are welcome! If you’re new to GitHub, check out the [GitHub Guides](https://guides.github.com). Fork this repo, make your changes, and open a pull request. We’re happy to help beginners.

You'll know it worked when the text encourages new contributors and includes a link to learning resources.

---

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake**: Using vague language like “easy to use” or “fast”.
  **Fix**: Replace it with a specific benefit, e.g., “runs in under 2 seconds on most computers”.
- **Mistake**: Forgetting to save the file after editing.
  **Fix**: Always click **Commit changes** at the bottom of the editor after each major section.
- **Mistake**: Writing long paragraphs under headings.
  **Fix**: Keep each section to 2–4 short sentences. Use bullet points for lists.

---

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: You can now share your coding projects with friends, teachers, or future employers with a polished README. No more blank pages or awkward explanations.
- **For your business or work**: A clear README saves time in onboarding new team members and makes your open-source tools more attractive to contributors and clients.
- **If you're just getting started**: This is your first step toward building a portfolio of projects you can show off with pride.

---

## Try it now
Open your GitHub repository, create or edit the `README.md` file, and use the **Ask Copilot** button to generate a structure. Replace the placeholders with your project’s details, then commit the changes. You now have a professional README ready to share!
